title: How heavy should each rice bag be, and how many bags?
description: Two heaps of rice, eighty four and one hundred and eight kilograms, are packed in equal bags. The factors of each weight are listed, the shared ones are picked, and the largest gives the fewest bags. Keeko's doubt, one big bag from each farm, is weighed and struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: equal bags for two heaps need a common factor of both weights, and the largest common factor needs the fewest bags. Watch for students who count one bag per farm and forget that the bags must weigh the same.

source: Lekhana has 84 kg and 108 kg of rice from two farms. Find th
video_script.why: The child can list common factors but has not yet used them for a second real situation, or counted what the best factor gives.
video_script.substitution: A bag weight that packs a heap exactly is a factor of the heap, so the weight for both heaps is a common factor.
video_script.anchor: Two heaps of rice, eighty four kilograms and one hundred and eight kilograms, packed in equal bags.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says two bags, one big bag from each farm. Those bags would weigh 84 and 108 kg, which are not equal.

final_answer.spoken: each bag weighs twelve kilograms and sixteen bags are needed

names.{{NAME_6}}: buys rice from two farms (84 kg and 108 kg) and packs it in bags

maths_rules: Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Fewest bags means the heaviest bag, 12 kg.
Bags from the first farm: 84 / 12 = 7. Bags from the second farm: 108 / 12 = 9.
Slip: two bags would weigh 84 kg and 108 kg, which are not equal.
video_script.design: One idea: the bag weight is a common factor of both heaps, and the largest one gives the fewest bags. Assumes factor lists and division. Wrong idea: one big bag per farm. The two heaps stay on the board all video.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about {{NAME_6}}, who buys rice from two farms.

<bookmark mark='farms'/>One farm gives eighty four kilograms, and the other gives one hundred and eight kilograms. <bookmark mark='bags'/>Each bag has rice from one farm only, and all bags weigh the same whole number of kilograms.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What should each bag weigh, and how many bags are needed?

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>A heap is packed exactly when the bag weight divides the heap.
<bookmark mark='factor'/>The bag weight must be a factor of the heap.
<bookmark mark='both'/>Both heaps use the same bag weight, so it must be a common factor of both.

narration: <bookmark mark='f84a'/>Step one, list the factors of each weight. The factors of eighty four are one, two, three, four, six and seven.
<bookmark mark='f84b'/>They go on with twelve, fourteen, twenty one, twenty eight, forty two and eighty four.
<bookmark mark='f108a'/>The factors of one hundred and eight are one, two, three, four, six and nine.
<bookmark mark='f108b'/>Then come twelve, eighteen, twenty seven, thirty six, fifty four and one hundred and eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='both'/>Step two, pick the numbers that are on both lists, because the bag weight must suit both farms.

{{NAME_6}} needs sixteen bags in all.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.
<bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks two bags are enough, one big bag from each farm.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Those bags would weigh eighty four and one hundred and eight kilograms. They are not equal, and equal bags are what is wanted.
